When they do exercise a power, they must generally give their name, their place of duty and the reason for using it. Detention is limited as well: after arrest a person may be held to investigate their involvement only for a limited 'investigation period', which can be extended only by a detention warrant, so longer detention is subject to independent oversight. Detained people also have rights, including to communicate with a friend, relative or lawyer, and additional protections apply to vulnerable people such as children. The courts add a safeguard after the event, because under the Evidence Act 1995 (NSW) a court may exclude evidence obtained improperly or in breach of the law.

questions.text: Analyse the impact of technology on the investigation of crime.

Explains the impact of technology on investigation, with relevant examples

Surveillance technology and the warrant requirement
Benefits: identifying offenders, linking crimes, excluding innocent suspects
Issues: privacy, bodily integrity, error or contamination, new forms of offending
How the law balances these, and an overall judgement
questions.model:
Technology has made police far better at solving crime, but every gain in investigative power is also a new way into people's private lives. Whether its impact is positive overall comes down to the legal safeguards around it.

Take DNA. Profiling can identify an offender from a trace sample, link separate crimes and, importantly, exclude innocent suspects. The Crimes (Forensic Procedures) Act 2000 (NSW) regulates when samples may be taken from suspects, offenders and volunteers, requiring consent or an order in many cases, and governs how DNA profiles are used and when they must be destroyed. The Act is essentially a compromise between investigative efficiency and a suspect's bodily integrity and privacy.

Surveillance cuts both ways in the same way. Listening, optical, tracking and data surveillance devices allow police to gather evidence of organised and covert offending that would otherwise be very difficult to prove. Because covert surveillance is highly intrusive, the Surveillance Devices Act 2007 (NSW) generally requires police to obtain a warrant, placing independent judicial control over its use.

Technology is not only a tool for police, though. Offenders use encrypted communications and online platforms, and forensic evidence can be contaminated or misinterpreted, so it is not infallible. Its value at trial depends on proper procedures, and evidence obtained improperly may be excluded under the Evidence Act 1995 (NSW).

Technology has clearly strengthened investigation. Its benefits for justice, though, last only as long as the legal limits that protect suspects and the wider community are respected.

questions.text: Explain the role of the jury in the criminal trial process in NSW.

questions.model:
In NSW, juries are used mainly in trials for serious indictable offences in the District and Supreme Courts. In the adversary system the jury is the finder of fact: after hearing the evidence and the judge's directions on the law, the jurors decide whether the prosecution has proved the accused's guilt beyond reasonable doubt and return the verdict. The judge decides questions of law, rules on the admissibility of evidence and, if there is a conviction, imposes the sentence.

Jurors are drawn at random from the community under the Jury Act 1977 (NSW), which also sets out who is ineligible or may be excused and allows the parties a limited number of challenges. That puts ordinary members of the community at the centre of criminal justice, which is the whole point of being judged by one's peers. Verdicts are normally unanimous, but the Act allows majority verdicts in limited circumstances, after a minimum period of deliberation, which reduces the cost and delay of hung juries.

Juries are not used in every case, though. Under the Criminal Procedure Act 1986 (NSW) a trial may be heard by a judge alone in some circumstances, for example where prejudicial publicity raises concerns about a jury's impartiality. So the jury matters as a safeguard of community participation and fairness, but the system accepts that it has to be weighed against the risks of prejudice, cost and delay.

questions.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of reforms to the rule against double jeopardy in achieving justice.

criteria.descriptor: Makes an informed judgement about the effectiveness of double jeopardy reforms in achieving justice; explains the reasons for and the effect of the reforms, balancing the rights of the accused against the interests of victims and society; uses relevant legislation and cases

questions.model:
The rule against double jeopardy protects a person from being tried twice for the same offence. It promotes finality, stops the state using its greater resources to prosecute a person repeatedly, and supports public confidence in verdicts. However, an absolute rule can produce injustice where compelling evidence of guilt appears after an acquittal.

R v Carroll (2002) 213 CLR 635 brought that tension into the open. After the accused's murder conviction was overturned on appeal and an acquittal entered, he was later prosecuted for perjury for denying the killing at his trial. The High Court held the perjury prosecution was an abuse of process because it sought to controvert the acquittal. The decision prompted public debate and law reform across Australia.

In NSW, amendments made in 2006 to the Crimes (Appeal and Review) Act 2001 (NSW) created exceptions that allow the Court of Criminal Appeal to order the retrial of an acquitted person for certain very serious offences where there is fresh and compelling evidence, or where the acquittal was tainted, for example by an offence against the administration of justice, and a retrial is in the interests of justice. This deals effectively with the rare case where finality would protect a guilty person, which serves victims, their families and community confidence.

Importantly, the accused still keeps strong protection. The exceptions are limited to very serious offences and require an order of an appellate court, so acquittals cannot be reopened routinely. Critics argue, however, that any exception weakens the finality of verdicts and could reduce the pressure on investigators to be thorough the first time.

In my view the reforms are largely effective. They let the worst miscarriages produced by an absolute rule be corrected without opening the door to abuse of state power, and their real test will be how sparingly they are used.

questions.text: Discuss the role of judicial discretion in sentencing offenders.

criteria.descriptor: Presents a balanced discussion of judicial discretion in sentencing, including its benefits for individualised justice and its risk of inconsistency; refers accurately to legislation and cases; uses legal terminology precisely
Discusses the role of discretion with some balance and some relevant legal support
Describes how judges sentence, with limited discussion

required_elements: Discretion operates within statutory limits: maximum penalties, purposes, aggravating and mitigating factors
Instinctive synthesis as the method of weighing factors
Guidance that structures discretion (standard non-parole periods) and its limits
Proportionality as a limit on sentence length
Arguments for (individualised justice) and against (inconsistency, public confidence); appeals as a check
questions.model:
Judicial discretion is the judge's power to decide the right sentence within the limits Parliament sets. Without it, individual justice would be impossible; with it comes the risk of inconsistency, which both Parliament and the courts have tried to rein in.

Discretion operates within a statutory framework. Parliament sets maximum penalties, and the Crimes (Sentencing Procedure) Act 1999 (NSW) sets out the purposes of sentencing, such as punishment, deterrence, community protection, rehabilitation and denunciation, and lists aggravating and mitigating factors the court must take into account. Within that framework, the High Court in Markarian v The Queen (2005) 228 CLR 357 endorsed 'instinctive synthesis', where the judge weighs all relevant factors together to reach a single sentence. That lets the court respond to the circumstances of the offence and the offender, such as remorse, prospects of rehabilitation, or the profound childhood deprivation recognised as relevant in Bugmy v The Queen (2013) 249 CLR 571.

Discretion is also constrained by principle. In Veen v The Queen (No 2) (1988) 164 CLR 465 the High Court held that a sentence must not exceed what is proportionate to the gravity of the offence merely to protect society. Even when public concern is running high, an offender cannot be punished beyond what the offence deserves.

The usual criticism is that similar offences can attract different sentences, which can undermine public confidence and lead to claims that sentences are too lenient. Parliament has responded with guidance such as standard non-parole periods, but in Muldrock v The Queen (2011) 244 CLR 120 the High Court held that a standard non-parole period is one guidepost and not a mandatory starting point, preserving the judge's overall discretion. More rigid approaches, such as mandatory minimum sentences, reduce inconsistency but risk unjust outcomes because they stop the court considering individual circumstances.

Appeals are the other check: both the offender and the prosecution can appeal against a sentence, which allows appellate courts to correct errors and promote consistency.

Discretion is essential to individualised justice. Its risks are real, but they are better handled through principle, guidance and appeals than by taking discretion away.

questions.model:
A young person questioned by police has the same basic rights as an adult, plus extra protection because of their age and vulnerability. The starting point is the right to silence: a young person apart from giving certain identifying details when required, they do not have to answer questions, and they must be cautioned that anything they say may be used in evidence. Under the framework of the Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002 (NSW), children are treated as vulnerable persons, so a support person, such as a parent or another adult who is not a police officer, should be present during questioning, and the young person can contact a lawyer.

The extra protection matters because young people may not understand their rights or the consequences of what they say, and may be more easily pressured. The Children (Criminal Proceedings) Act 1987 (NSW) reinforces them: statements or admissions made by a child without a suitable adult present may be excluded at trial unless the court is satisfied there was a proper and sufficient reason for that person's absence. These rules reflect the Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989), which requires that children accused of offences be treated in a way that takes account of their age and the desirability of their reintegration into society. questions.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of the law relating to the age of criminal responsibility in achieving justice for young people.

criteria.descriptor: Makes an informed judgement about the effectiveness of the law on the age of criminal responsibility; explains the conclusive presumption and doli incapax accurately; integrates relevant legislation, cases, international standards and reform debate
Makes a sound judgement with relevant legal support
Describes the age of criminal responsibility and doli incapax, with some judgement
Provides general information about young offenders or the age of responsibility

required_elements: The conclusive presumption for children under 10
Doli incapax for children aged 10 to 13 and the test in RP v The Queen [2016] HCA 53
The international standard in the Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) and its committee's recommended minimum age
Practical limits of doli incapax (arrest, remand and court before it is tested)
The law reform debate (raising the age, alternative responses) and an explicit judgement
questions.model:
The age of criminal responsibility is a balancing act: children's capacity for moral judgement is still developing, yet the community has a legitimate interest in responding to harmful behaviour. NSW gets that balance only partly right, which is why the issue remains the subject of serious reform debate.

Under the Children (Criminal Proceedings) Act 1987 (NSW) there is a conclusive presumption that a child under 10 cannot commit an offence. For children aged 10 to 13, the common law presumption of doli incapax applies: the child is presumed incapable of criminal responsibility unless the prosecution proves beyond reasonable doubt that the child knew the act was seriously wrong. In RP v The Queen [2016] HCA 53 the High Court made clear that this requires proof that the child understood the conduct was seriously wrong in a moral sense, as distinct from merely naughty or mischievous, and that the presumption must be rebutted by evidence about the particular child. That is a genuine safeguard, because it stops a child being convicted simply because they did the act.

The trouble is that doli incapax is tested at trial, so a child aged 10 to 13 can still be arrested, held on remand and brought before a court before the presumption is considered. Evidence used to rebut it may also draw on the child's family circumstances and disadvantage, which raises fairness concerns.

International law gives a useful benchmark. The Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) requires states to set a minimum age below which children are presumed not to have the capacity to infringe the criminal law, and to deal with children without resorting to judicial proceedings wherever appropriate. Its monitoring committee has recommended a minimum age of at least 14. Measured against that standard, a minimum age of 10 is low.

Law reform has been debated across Australia, with some jurisdictions raising or committing to raise the minimum age and others choosing not to. Supporters of raising the age argue that early contact with the criminal justice system can entrench offending and that welfare, health and education responses are better suited to young children. Opponents argue that a higher age could leave serious harmful conduct without an adequate response, and that doli incapax already protects children who lack understanding.

My judgement is that the law is only partly effective in achieving justice for young people. Doli incapax, as clarified in RP v The Queen, is a real safeguard, but the low minimum age sits below the international benchmark and exposes young children to the criminal process. Raising the age, combined with well-resourced alternative responses to harmful behaviour, would better reflect the Convention's emphasis on dealing with children outside the courts wherever appropriate.

questions.model: Crimes against the international community are the most serious crimes of concern to humanity as a whole, such as genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression. They are recognised in international law and can be prosecuted by the International Criminal Court under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (1998), as well as by national courts. Transnational crimes are a different category: offences that cross national borders, such as drug trafficking, people smuggling, human trafficking and cybercrime. questions.text: Assess the impact of state sovereignty on the effectiveness of measures to deal with international crime.

criteria.descriptor: Makes an informed judgement about the impact of state sovereignty on dealing with international crime; explains how sovereignty both limits and enables international and domestic measures; supports the argument with relevant treaties, legislation and cases
Explains the role of state sovereignty, with some judgement and examples
Provides general statements about sovereignty or international crime

required_elements: A definition of state sovereignty

Complementarity gives states primary responsibility
Domestic measures as exercises of sovereignty (legislation, extradition)
An explicit judgement about the overall impact
questions.model:
State sovereignty is the principle that each state has supreme authority over its territory and people and cannot be bound by international law without its consent. Mostly, sovereignty limits the effectiveness of international measures against crime. It also cuts the other way, though, because it leaves states with the primary responsibility to act.

You can see the limiting effect most clearly in the International Criminal Court. The Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (1998) is a treaty, so it binds only the states that become parties, and the Court's jurisdiction generally depends on the crime occurring on a state party's territory or being committed by a national of a state party, unless the Security Council refers a situation. Several powerful states are not parties. The Court also has no police force: it relies on states to arrest and surrender suspects, so where a state refuses to cooperate, arrest warrants can remain unenforced for years.

Sovereignty is even written into the Court's design through complementarity: a case is inadmissible where a state is genuinely investigating or prosecuting it. That respects sovereignty while pushing states to prosecute international crimes themselves.

At the domestic level, sovereignty is what makes action possible. Australia has used its law-making power to enact the International Criminal Court Act 2002 (Cth), allowing it to cooperate with the Court, and to include genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes, as well as transnational offences such as people trafficking, in the Criminal Code Act 1995 (Cth). For transnational crime, cooperation depends on arrangements between states, and the Extradition Act 1988 (Cth) allows extradition to be refused on specified grounds, reflecting each state's control over its own legal processes.

State sovereignty therefore substantially limits international measures, which can only ever be as strong as the consent and cooperation behind them. Where a state chooses to use its sovereignty to legislate and cooperate, though, domestic measures can be highly effective.

questions.text: Describe the development of formal statements of human rights after the Second World War.

questions.model:
Before the Second World War, human rights were largely a matter for each state's domestic law. The atrocities of the war changed that, and states began to treat human rights as a matter of international concern. The Charter of the United Nations (1945) included among the purposes of the United Nations promoting and encouraging respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms for all.

The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948), adopted by the UN General Assembly, was the first comprehensive international statement of rights, covering civil and political rights as well as economic, social and cultural rights. Because a declaration is not binding, the next step was binding treaties. In 1966 the General Assembly adopted the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (1966). Together with the Declaration, these are known as the International Bill of Rights.

Later treaties then focused on particular groups or issues, such as the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (1979), the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (1984) and the Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989). Each has a committee of independent experts to monitor it, which shows the system moving from stating principles to checking whether states actually comply.

Customary international law is unwritten: it develops when states consistently follow a practice because they believe they are legally obliged to do so, and it can bind states that have not ratified a relevant treaty. questions.text: Explain how Australian courts protect human rights in the absence of a national bill of rights.

criteria.descriptor: Explains clearly how courts protect human rights through the Constitution, the common law and statutory interpretation, with relevant cases, and identifies limits
Explains how courts protect human rights, with relevant examples
Describes some ways courts protect rights

required_elements: Express constitutional rights enforced by the High Court
Implied constitutional rights: Lange (political communication) and Roach (voting)
Common law protection: Mabo (No 2) and Dietrich
Statutory interpretation and its limits (Momcilovic)
Limits: Parliament can override common law rights; courts act only on cases brought
questions.model:
Without a national bill of rights, Australian courts have to protect human rights indirectly, through the Constitution, the common law and the way they read statutes.

The High Court enforces the few express rights in the Australian Constitution, such as trial by jury for indictable Commonwealth offences (s 80), freedom of religion from Commonwealth laws (s 116) and acquisition of property on just terms (s 51(xxxi)). It has also found rights implied by the Constitution's structure. In Lange v Australian Broadcasting Corporation (1997) 189 CLR 520 the Court confirmed an implied freedom of political communication, and in Roach v Electoral Commissioner (2007) 233 CLR 162 it held invalid a law that removed the vote from all prisoners serving full-time sentences. Both decisions put real limits on what governments can do.

The common law does similar work. In Mabo v Queensland (No 2) (1992) 175 CLR 1 the High Court recognised native title, and in Dietrich v The Queen (1992) 177 CLR 292 it held that a serious criminal trial may be stayed where an accused cannot obtain representation through no fault of their own, protecting the right to a fair trial.

Courts also read legislation consistently with rights where they can, and statutory human rights Acts in Victoria, the ACT and Queensland require this. Momcilovic v The Queen (2011) 245 CLR 1 shows where that stops: interpretation cannot rewrite a law. Because Parliament can override common law rights by clear words, and courts act only when a case is brought, judicial protection of rights in Australia is real but limited.

questions.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of the United Nations in promoting and enforcing human rights.

criteria.descriptor: Makes an informed judgement about the effectiveness of the United Nations in promoting and enforcing human rights; analyses strengths and limitations of UN bodies and mechanisms; supports the argument with relevant treaties, bodies and examples
Makes a sound judgement with relevant examples
Describes UN bodies, with limited judgement

required_elements: Standard-setting: the Charter, the Declaration and the binding covenants
Monitoring: treaty committees and the Universal Periodic Review
Individual complaints: the First Optional Protocol, Toonen and Australia's response
Limits: state sovereignty, non-binding views, Security Council veto
An explicit judgement distinguishing promotion from enforcement
questions.model:
The United Nations is highly effective at promoting human rights and much less effective at enforcing them. It can set standards and monitor states, but almost everything it does depends on the consent and cooperation of sovereign states.

Standard-setting is where the UN has achieved the most. The Charter of the United Nations (1945) made the promotion of human rights one of the organisation's purposes, and the UN then developed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) and binding treaties such as the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966). These instruments give governments, courts, NGOs and individuals a shared benchmark for judging state conduct.

Monitoring comes next. Treaty committees review periodic reports from states parties, and the United Nations Human Rights Council conducts the Universal Periodic Review, in which every UN member state's record is examined by other states. These processes do expose shortcomings and produce recommendations, but in the end they run on peer pressure: a state can ignore recommendations without legal consequence, and the Council's decisions can be shaped by political alliances.

Individual complaints show what enforcement can achieve, and where it runs out. Under the Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966), individuals can complain to the Human Rights Committee. In Toonen v Australia (UN Human Rights Committee, 1994) the Committee found that Tasmanian laws criminalising consensual sex between adult men breached the right to privacy, and the Commonwealth responded with the Human Rights (Sexual Conduct) Act 1994 (Cth). Yet the Committee's views are not binding, and compliance depends on the political will of the state concerned.

Coercive action through the Security Council is possible only where violations threaten international peace and security, and any permanent member can veto it, so responses to serious violations are often slow or blocked.

The UN is an effective promoter of human rights and a genuine source of diplomatic and moral pressure, but state sovereignty keeps its enforcement role weak. In the end its success depends on states turning international standards into domestic law, as Australia did after Toonen.

questions.text: Analyse the tension between state sovereignty and the protection of human rights in relation to ONE contemporary human rights issue you have studied.

criteria.descriptor: Analyses the tension between state sovereignty and human rights protection in a specific contemporary issue, showing cause and effect, with accurate legal examples

questions.model:
State sovereignty means each state has supreme authority over its own territory, and nowhere does that collide more obviously with human rights than in the treatment of asylum seekers. A state has a sovereign right to decide who comes in, yet it has also accepted international obligations towards people fleeing persecution.

Australia is a party to the Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees (1951), which defines a refugee and obliges states not to return refugees to places where their life or freedom would be threatened (non-refoulement). What the Convention does not do is tell states how to process claims. Australia has exercised its sovereignty through the Migration Act 1958 (Cth), which requires the detention of unlawful non-citizens. Critics, including UN bodies and NGOs, argue that mandatory detention conflicts with the right to liberty, while governments justify it as necessary for border control and security.

In Australia, the courts have been where this tension is actually worked out. In Al-Kateb v Godwin (2004) 219 CLR 562 a majority of the High Court upheld detention that might continue indefinitely. In NZYQ v Minister for Immigration, Citizenship and Multicultural Affairs (2023) the High Court overruled Al-Kateb, holding that detention cannot validly continue where there is no real prospect of removal in the reasonably foreseeable future. So on this issue the most effective check on sovereign power has come from domestic constitutional limits, not from international law.

The tension has not gone away. International standards set the expectations, but they cannot be enforced against a sovereign state, so asylum seekers' protection still rests on domestic courts and political will.

questions.model:
Several international instruments deal with the use of child soldiers. The Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) requires states to take all feasible measures to ensure that children under 15 do not take a direct part in hostilities, and to refrain from recruiting children under 15 into their armed forces. The Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child on the involvement of children in armed conflict (2000) lifted the standard: states parties must take all feasible measures to ensure that members of their armed forces under 18 do not take a direct part in hostilities, and must ensure that people under 18 are not compulsorily recruited, while armed groups distinct from a state's armed forces should not recruit or use people under 18 in hostilities.

International criminal law goes a step further and makes individuals responsible. Under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (1998), conscripting or enlisting children under 15, or using them to participate actively in hostilities, is a war crime. The Court's first trial judgment, Prosecutor v Thomas Lubanga Dyilo (ICC, 2012), convicted a militia leader of these crimes in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which proved the framework can be enforced against individuals. Australia is a party to these treaties and has included war crimes in the Criminal Code Act 1995 (Cth), so such conduct can also be prosecuted domestically.

questions.text: Explain how defences can remove or reduce criminal liability. Refer to at least ONE complete defence and ONE partial defence.

questions.model:
Even when the prosecution proves the act, a defence can mean the accused escapes liability altogether or is convicted of something less serious. A complete defence means the person is not criminally responsible at all, and self-defence is the main example: under the Crimes Act 1900 (NSW), a person is not criminally responsible if they believed their conduct was necessary to defend themselves or another person and it was a reasonable response in the circumstances as they perceived them. Once there is evidence of self-defence, the prosecution must disprove it beyond reasonable doubt. Another complete defence is mental health or cognitive impairment under the Mental Health and Cognitive Impairment Forensic Provisions Act 2020 (NSW), which leads to the special verdict 'act proven but not criminally responsible' and allows the court to make orders to protect the community.

A partial defence works differently. It applies only to murder and, if it succeeds, reduces the conviction to manslaughter. In NSW the partial defences include extreme provocation and substantial impairment by abnormality of mind. The idea is that a person who kills in these circumstances is less morally culpable than a person who kills intentionally without such circumstances, while still holding them responsible for a very serious crime. That way the criminal law can reflect real differences in moral blame instead of treating everyone who causes harm the same.

questions.model:
Discretion, the power to choose between options, runs through almost every stage of a criminal investigation. It is what lets the system respond sensibly to individual circumstances, and it is also where inconsistency and misuse can creep in.

It starts before police are even involved, because victims and witnesses decide whether to report a crime. Many offences come to the attention of police only through reports, so the community's willingness to report shapes which crimes are investigated.

Police then have to decide whether to investigate, whom to approach and whether to use coercive powers. Under the Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002 (NSW), powers such as search and arrest depend on an officer's assessment of reasonable suspicion, and arrest without a warrant also requires the officer to be satisfied that arrest is reasonably necessary. Officers can instead proceed by court attendance notice or, for young people, use warnings and cautions under the Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW). Choices like these let minor matters be dealt with proportionately and keep people out of custody.

Even after charge, discretion keeps operating. Police officers and courts make bail decisions under the Bail Act 2013 (NSW), weighing the risks posed by the accused, and prosecutors decide whether there is enough evidence to proceed.

No law can anticipate every situation, which is why discretion is valuable. But because individuals exercise it, it can be applied inconsistently or be influenced by bias, which is why safeguards such as the requirement for reasonable grounds, internal review and external oversight, for example by the Law Enforcement Conduct Commission, are important.

questions.text: Assess the effectiveness of alternative methods of sentencing, such as restorative justice, in achieving justice.

questions.model:
Alternative sentencing is largely effective: for many offenders and victims it achieves more than a conventional sentence could, mainly because it deals with why the person offended and brings the community into the process. How well it works, though, turns on who is eligible, how well it is resourced and how serious the offence is.

Restorative justice brings offenders, victims and the community together to acknowledge harm and agree on how to repair it. Circle sentencing, available in the Local Court for some Aboriginal offenders, involves Aboriginal Elders and community members working with the magistrate to decide on a sentence. Done well, it makes the process more culturally meaningful, increase the offender's sense of accountability to their community and give victims a voice. For young people, youth justice conferences under the Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW) apply similar principles as an alternative to court.

Community-based sentences, such as intensive correction orders, let an offender to serve a sentence in the community under supervision and conditions. Under the Crimes (Sentencing Procedure) Act 1999 (NSW), the court must still impose a sentence that reflects the purposes of sentencing, and these options support rehabilitation because the offender can keep employment and family ties and to address problems such as drug dependence.

Part of the case for these alternatives comes from the Pathways to Justice: Inquiry into the Incarceration Rate of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples (ALRC Report 133), which considered the over-representation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in prison and made recommendations on matters including sentencing options.

Alternatives are not a cure-all, though. They are generally unsuitable for the most serious offences, where denunciation and community protection require imprisonment. They depend on programs being available and funded, so access may be uneven. Some victims and members of the public also see them as too lenient.

For suitable offences, then, alternative methods are effective because they promote rehabilitation and repair harm. They sit alongside imprisonment; they do not replace it.

Complementarity: a court of last resort
An example such as the Lubanga case
Limits: reliance on states for arrests; non-party states
questions.model:
The International Criminal Court is a permanent international court established by the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (1998). Its role is to try individuals, including political and military leaders, for the most serious crimes of concern to the international community: genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression. The point is that individuals, not just states, answer for these crimes.

The Court's jurisdiction generally depends on the crime being committed on the territory of a state party or by a national of a state party, although the Security Council can refer a situation in any state. A case can begin through a referral by a state party or the Security Council, or by the Prosecutor acting on their own initiative with the approval of the Court's judges.

Importantly, it is a court of last resort. Under the principle of complementarity, a case is inadmissible where a state with jurisdiction is genuinely investigating or prosecuting it, so national courts keep the primary role. The Court's first trial judgment, Prosecutor v Thomas Lubanga Dyilo (ICC, 2012), convicted a militia leader of enlisting, conscripting and using child soldiers, which showed it can hold individuals to account.

Its biggest weakness is that it depends on states. It has no police force, so it relies on states to arrest and surrender suspects, and states that are not parties to the Rome Statute generally have no obligation to cooperate.
evidence_titles: Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (1998)

questions.text: Explain the significance of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in the development of human rights.

criteria.descriptor: Explains clearly why the Declaration was significant, including its content, its legal status and its influence on later binding law
Explains the significance of the Declaration with some detail
Describes the Declaration
Provides some relevant information

required_elements: The first comprehensive international statement of rights, adopted by the General Assembly in 1948
Covers civil and political as well as economic, social and cultural rights
Not binding in itself
Influence: the two covenants (International Bill of Rights), later treaties, customary law, domestic law
questions.model:
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) was the first comprehensive international statement of the rights that belong to every person. Adopted by the UN General Assembly after the Second World War, it gave effect to the commitment in the Charter of the United Nations (1945) to promote respect for human rights, and it recognised both civil and political rights, such as freedom of expression and a fair trial, and economic, social and cultural rights, such as education and an adequate standard of living.

As a General Assembly declaration, it was not binding in itself. Its real significance is the influence it has had. Its rights were developed into binding treaties, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (1966), which together with the Declaration form the International Bill of Rights. It has also shaped later treaties, national constitutions and laws, and some of its provisions are now regarded as part of customary international law. That is why the Declaration is seen as the moment human rights became universal standards instead of matters left entirely to each state.

International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (1966)

questions.text: Assess the effectiveness of statutory bills of rights in protecting human rights in Australian jurisdictions.

criteria.descriptor: Makes an informed judgement about the effectiveness of statutory bills of rights; explains how they operate and their limits; supports the argument with relevant legislation and cases
Describes statutory bills of rights with some judgement and relevant examples
Provides general information about the protection of rights in Australia

required_elements: Which jurisdictions have statutory bills of rights (ACT, Victoria, Queensland)
How they operate: compatibility statements, rights-consistent interpretation, obligations on public authorities, declarations
Parliamentary sovereignty: declarations do not invalidate laws
Limits shown by Momcilovic; limited remedies; no national equivalent
An explicit judgement
questions.model:
Where they exist, statutory bills of rights are moderately effective. They build rights into law-making and government decision-making, but they are deliberately designed to leave Parliament with the final say.

Three jurisdictions have such laws: the Human Rights Act 2004 (ACT), the Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities Act 2006 (Vic) and the Human Rights Act 2019 (Qld). Each requires statements of compatibility for new bills, requires laws to be interpreted compatibly with human rights where possible, and imposes obligations on public authorities to act compatibly with human rights. The Supreme Court can declare that a law cannot be interpreted compatibly with human rights, which requires a government response but does not affect the law's validity.

Their main strength is the culture of rights they encourage. Compatibility statements force governments to explain why a law limits rights, and obligations on public authorities shape everyday decisions in areas such as housing, health and policing, which may prevent breaches before they occur.

Their legal force is a different story. In Momcilovic v The Queen (2011) 245 CLR 1 the High Court held that the Victorian Charter's interpretation provision operates within the ordinary limits of statutory interpretation and does not allow courts to rewrite legislation. Parliament can pass laws that are incompatible with rights, and remedies for individuals are limited. At the federal level, the Human Rights (Parliamentary Scrutiny) Act 2011 (Cth) provides only a scrutiny process, and NSW has no statutory bill of rights, so protection depends on where a person lives.

As a dialogue model, statutory bills of rights genuinely improve law-making and administration. They are much less effective when Parliament is determined to limit rights, or when an individual needs a strong remedy.

Media: awareness and public pressure

questions.model:
Laws alone have not stopped the use of child soldiers, and non-legal measures do much of the practical work alongside instruments such as the Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) and the Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child on the involvement of children in armed conflict (2000).

Non-government organisations document the recruitment and use of children by interviewing former child soldiers and reporting on armed groups. That evidence raises awareness, feeds into the work of UN bodies and can later support prosecutions. NGO advocacy has also helped push states to adopt and ratify stronger standards.

The media carries this work to a wider audience. Reporting on child soldiers brings the issue to international attention and can create public and diplomatic pressure on governments and on states that support armed groups.

UN agencies and community organisations run programs to help released children recover, return to school and reunite with their families. This is harm that punishing offenders cannot repair on its own, so these programs fill a real gap.

Their weakness is that they cannot compel armed groups or states to comply. Their effectiveness depends on funding, access to conflict areas and the willingness of governments to respond to pressure, so they work best alongside legal measures.

questions.text: With reference to the hypothetical scenario, explain whether the elements of a criminal offence could be established against Jake.

stimulus.title: Hypothetical scenario: the shove outside the cafe
stimulus.body:
This scenario is invented for practice. It does not describe real people or events.

Late one night, Jake (aged 24) argues with Chris outside a cafe. Witnesses say Chris swung a punch at Jake, who stepped back and then shoved Chris hard in the chest with both hands. Chris fell backwards, hit his head on the kerb and was taken to hospital with a fractured skull. He has since recovered.

Jake tells police: 'I just wanted him to back off. He'd already thrown a punch and I thought he was going to hit me again. I never meant for him to get hurt like that.'

Jake has been charged with a serious assault offence under the Crimes Act 1900 (NSW).

criteria.descriptor: Applies the elements of crime (actus reus, mens rea, causation) and the burden and standard of proof accurately to the scenario, and explains the relevance of self-defence
Explains the elements of crime with clear reference to the scenario
Describes the elements of crime with some reference to the scenario
Outlines actus reus and/or mens rea
Provides some relevant information

required_elements: Burden and standard of proof on the prosecution
Actus reus: the voluntary shove and the resulting injury
Causation: the shove as a substantial and operating cause of the fracture
Mens rea: intention or recklessness, using Jake's statement
Self-defence: belief that the conduct was necessary and a reasonable response; the prosecution must disprove it
questions.model:
To convict Jake, the prosecution must prove each element of the offence beyond reasonable doubt; Jake does not have to prove his innocence, as Woolmington v DPP [1935] AC 462 established.

Start with the actus reus, the physical element. Jake's voluntary act of shoving Chris in the chest is an application of force, and the prosecution would rely on the witnesses who saw it. It must also prove causation: that the shove was a substantial and operating cause of Chris's fractured skull. Although the injury happened when Chris hit the kerb, the fall was a direct result of the shove, so causation would probably be established.

The mens rea, or mental element, is harder. Jake's statement that he 'just wanted him to back off' suggests he intended to push Chris, but not to cause serious injury. Whether the mental element is proved depends on what the particular offence under the Crimes Act 1900 (NSW) requires, such as intention or recklessness as to a certain kind of harm, so his claim that he 'never meant' the injury is relevant but not necessarily decisive.

The real problem for the prosecution is self-defence. Chris had already thrown a punch, and Jake says he feared another blow. In NSW a person is not criminally responsible if they believed their conduct was necessary to defend themselves and it was a reasonable response in the circumstances as they perceived them. Once there is evidence of self-defence, the prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt that Jake was not acting in self-defence. Stepping back and pushing, rather than striking, may be seen as a reasonable response to a punch, which would make a conviction difficult.

The actus reus and causation are likely to be proved, but self-defence leaves a real doubt about whether Jake is criminally responsible.

questions.text: With reference to the hypothetical scenario, assess whether the police exercised their powers lawfully and fairly, and the possible consequences for the evidence against Lily.

stimulus.title: Hypothetical scenario: the search at the train station
stimulus.body:
This scenario is invented for practice. It does not describe real people or events.

Officer Grant sees Lily (aged 19) standing near a train station exit. The officer has no information about Lily and later says she 'just had a feeling'. Without giving her name, place of duty or a reason, she tells Lily to empty her bag. Lily refuses. Officer Grant takes the bag and finds a small quantity of a prohibited drug.

Lily is arrested and taken to the police station. She asks to call a lawyer but is told she can do that 'after we've had a chat'. She is then interviewed for several hours without a break, and admits that the drug is hers. The interview is recorded.

criteria.descriptor: Makes an informed judgement about the lawfulness and fairness of the police conduct; applies the relevant police powers and safeguards accurately to the scenario; explains the possible consequences for the evidence
Identifies some breaches of police powers or rights with reference to the scenario and some legal support
Provides general information about police powers

required_elements: A search without a warrant needs reasonable suspicion; a 'feeling' is not enough
The safeguards were not followed (name, place of duty and reason not given)
Rights after arrest: delayed access to a lawyer; length of detention and questioning
The discretion to exclude improperly or illegally obtained evidence (the drug and the admission)
A judgement about lawfulness and the likely outcome; a possible complaint
questions.model:
The police broke the rules more than once here, so Lily's rights were inadequately protected, and that puts the key evidence against her at real risk of being excluded.

The search itself was probably unlawful. Under the Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002 (NSW), police may search a person without a warrant only if they suspect on reasonable grounds that the person has something such as a prohibited drug. Reasonable suspicion must rest on facts or circumstances, not a hunch. Officer Grant had no information about Lily and acted on 'just a feeling', so the requirement was not met. She also failed to give her name, place of duty and the reason for the search, safeguards that the Act generally requires so that people know who is exercising power over them and why.

What happened after the arrest is just as concerning. A detained person has the right to communicate with a lawyer, and police should not put that off simply to obtain an interview. The Act also limits how long a person may be detained for investigation before being charged or released, unless a detention warrant extends the period. Several hours of questioning without a break, after Lily's request for a lawyer was refused, suggests the safeguards were not respected and that the admission may not have been freely made.

All of this matters at trial. Under the Evidence Act 1995 (NSW), a court may exclude evidence obtained improperly or in contravention of the law unless the desirability of admitting it outweighs the undesirability of admitting evidence obtained in that way. The court would weigh the seriousness of the breaches, and whether they were deliberate, against the importance of the evidence and the gravity of the offence. Because the offence involves a small quantity of a drug and the breaches were serious, there is a strong argument for excluding both the drug and the admission. Although recording the interview helps prove what was said, it does not cure the earlier unlawfulness.

In short, the police did not exercise their powers lawfully or fairly. Lily could also complain about the officer's conduct to the NSW Police Force or the Law Enforcement Conduct Commission.
questions.currency_note: Before you rely on this: Search powers, detention limits and the rights of detained persons are set out in the Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002 (NSW), which is amended from time to time. These details are stated as at the time of writing (October 2026) and may have changed; verify them against the current source before using them in an answer.

questions.text: Using the hypothetical data in the table, analyse how access to legal representation may affect the fairness of criminal trials.

stimulus.title: Hypothetical data: legal representation in a fictional District Court
stimulus.body:
The figures below are invented for practice. They do not describe any real court and must not be quoted as real statistics.

| Accused's representation (fictional court, one year) | Trials | Acquitted on all charges | Average trial length (days) | Appeals lodged |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Private lawyer | 120 | 42 | 6 | 18 |
| Legal aid lawyer | 300 | 84 | 5 | 30 |
| Self-represented | 30 | 3 | 9 | 9 |

Note (also invented): in this fictional court, self-represented accused were mostly charged with less serious indictable offences.

criteria.descriptor: Analyses the hypothetical data accurately to draw sound conclusions about legal representation and fairness; links the data to relevant legal principles and cases; recognises the limits of the data
Describes patterns in the data and links them to legal representation, with some legal support
Refers to the data or to legal representation in general terms

required_elements: Accurate use of the table (acquittals, trial length, appeals) without adding figures
Why representation matters in the adversary system
A link to Dietrich v The Queen (1992) 177 CLR 292 and the role of legal aid
The data shows an association, not proof of cause; other factors such as the seriousness of charges
A judgement about the effect on fairness
questions.model:
The hypothetical data points to legal representation making a real difference to both the outcome and the efficiency of trials, although figures like these cannot on their own prove that representation is the cause.

Acquittals show the clearest pattern. About one in three trials with a private lawyer, and just over one in four with a legal aid lawyer, ended in acquittal on all charges, compared with only one in ten for self-represented accused. That gap is striking because, according to the note, self-represented accused in this fictional court mostly faced less serious charges, which might be expected to favour them. It suggests that unrepresented accused struggle in the adversary system, in which each side must present its own case, test the other side's evidence through cross-examination and make legal submissions. Without legal knowledge, an accused may not recognise inadmissible evidence or available defences.

Efficiency seems to suffer as well. Trials of self-represented accused took the longest on average and produced the most appeals relative to the number of trials. Unrepresented accused may need more explanation from the judge, and errors at trial can lead to appeals, adding cost and delay for everyone, including victims and witnesses.

Private and legal aid lawyers are harder to compare. The acquittal figures differ, but the gap is much smaller than the gap with self-represented accused, and it could reflect differences in the types of cases rather than in the quality of representation. Legal aid lawyers appeared in most of the trials, which highlights how much the system depends on public funding.

These patterns support the principle in Dietrich v The Queen (1992) 177 CLR 292 that a trial for a serious offence may be unfair if the accused cannot obtain representation through no fault of their own. However, Dietrich does not create a right to publicly funded counsel, so access to representation depends heavily on legal aid funding. Taken together, the data links representation closely to fairness, but a real-world conclusion would need actual, verified statistics that account for the seriousness of the charges and the strength of the evidence.

questions.text: With reference to the hypothetical scenario, explain the factors a court would consider in sentencing Ben.

stimulus.title: Hypothetical scenario: the case of Ben
stimulus.body:
This scenario is invented for practice. It does not describe real people or events.

Ben (aged 22) has pleaded guilty, at the first available opportunity, to a break and enter offence. He broke into a home at night and stole electronic goods. The occupants, an elderly couple, woke to find him in their hallway. As he ran out, Ben pushed the husband aside; the husband fell but was not seriously hurt. A statement from the couple describes ongoing fear and difficulty sleeping.

Ben has two prior convictions for theft. He grew up in a household affected by violence and alcohol abuse and left school at 15. Since his arrest he has completed a residential drug rehabilitation program and has been offered a job. He has written a letter of apology to the couple.

criteria.descriptor: Explains clearly and accurately how aggravating and mitigating factors, the purposes of sentencing and relevant sentencing principles apply to the scenario
Explains some relevant factors with reference to the scenario
Identifies some factors or makes general statements about sentencing

required_elements: Aggravating features from the scenario (vulnerable victims in their home, force used, harm to the victims, prior record)
Mitigating features (early guilty plea, remorse, rehabilitation, deprived background and Bugmy)
Purposes of sentencing that pull in different directions
Method and limits: instinctive synthesis and proportionality
The role of the victims' account of harm
questions.model:
The court would weigh the circumstances of the offence and of Ben himself against the purposes of sentencing in the Crimes (Sentencing Procedure) Act 1999 (NSW), which include punishment, deterrence, protection of the community, rehabilitation, accountability, denunciation and recognising the harm done to the victims.

A number of things make this offence more serious. Breaking into a home at night while the occupants were present is a grave invasion of their security, and the victims were elderly, which the Act recognises as a form of vulnerability that aggravates an offence. Ben also used some force when he pushed the husband aside. The couple's statement describing ongoing fear helps the court understand the harm done. Ben's prior convictions for theft are relevant too: they cannot justify a heavier sentence than the offence deserves, but they reduce the leniency he might otherwise receive and point to a need for specific deterrence.

On the other side, several things favour leniency. Ben pleaded guilty at the first available opportunity, which spares the victims from giving evidence and usually entitles him to a reduced sentence. His letter of apology may show remorse. His completion of a residential rehabilitation program and his job offer suggest good prospects of rehabilitation. His upbringing in a household affected by violence and alcohol abuse is relevant under Bugmy v The Queen (2013) 249 CLR 571, where the High Court held that evidence of profound childhood deprivation may be taken into account and does not lose its relevance with time.

Here the purposes of sentencing pull against each other. Denunciation and general deterrence call for a firm response to a home invasion, while rehabilitation supports a sentence that does not undo Ben's progress. The judge would not add and subtract fixed amounts for each factor but would weigh them together through instinctive synthesis, as endorsed in Markarian v The Queen (2005) 228 CLR 357, and the final sentence must remain proportionate to the gravity of the offence, as required by Veen v The Queen (No 2) (1988) 164 CLR 465.

questions.text: With reference to the hypothetical data in the table, evaluate the effectiveness of diversionary options compared with court proceedings for young offenders.

stimulus.title: Hypothetical data: outcomes for young people in a fictional state
stimulus.body:
The figures below are invented for practice. They describe a fictional state, not NSW or any real place, and must not be quoted as real statistics.

| Pathway (young people aged 10 to 17, fictional state, one year) | Young people | Proceeded against again within 12 months | Average days from offence to finalisation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Police warning or caution | 4 000 | 800 | 20 |
| Youth justice conference | 1 000 | 250 | 90 |
| Court proceedings | 3 000 | 1 500 | 200 |

Note (also invented): in this fictional state, Aboriginal young people made up a larger share of the court pathway than of the warning and caution pathway.

criteria.descriptor: Makes an informed judgement about the effectiveness of diversion compared with court proceedings; uses the hypothetical data accurately and critically, recognising its limits; integrates relevant legislation and international standards
Makes a sound judgement using the data and relevant law
Describes diversion and refers to the data, with limited judgement
Provides general information about young offenders or diversion

required_elements: Accurate use of the table (further proceedings within 12 months; time to finalisation)
The diversion scheme in the Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW): warnings, cautions, conferences; an admission is required
Limits of the data: lower-risk young people are more likely to be diverted, so the data cannot prove cause
The equity concern raised by the note (unequal access to diversion)
The international standard in the Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) and an explicit judgement
questions.model:
On the hypothetical data, diversion beats court proceedings on both further offending and speed. The figures have real limits, though, and the note under the table raises a serious question about whether diversion is being applied fairly.

In NSW, the Young Offenders Act 1997 (NSW) creates a hierarchy of diversionary options: warnings, cautions and youth justice conferences, which deal with eligible young people outside the court system, usually after they admit the offence. Conferences bring together the young person, their family, the victim and others to agree on an outcome plan, reflecting restorative justice.

The table fits what the scheme is trying to do. About one in five young people given a warning or caution, and one in four who attended a conference, were proceeded against again within 12 months, compared with half of those dealt with by a court. Diversion was also much faster: warnings and cautions were finalised in an average of 20 days and conferences in 90, compared with 200 days for court matters. Speed matters for young people, because a long period awaiting court can disrupt schooling and family life, and a prompt response is more likely to be understood as a consequence of the behaviour.

What the data cannot show is that diversion caused the lower rate of further offending. Young people who are diverted are often first-time or less serious offenders, while those sent to court may already have a history of offending, so the groups are not comparable. A sound evaluation would compare similar young people who took different pathways.

The note is the most troubling part of the stimulus. If Aboriginal young people are less likely to receive warnings and cautions, they are more exposed to the court system, its delays and its risk of detention. This would undermine equality before the law, whatever the overall benefits of diversion.

Diversion also has the backing of international standards. The Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) encourages states to deal with children without resorting to judicial proceedings wherever appropriate and requires detention to be a last resort. Diversion is consistent with these standards because it limits young people's contact with the formal justice system.

My overall judgement is that diversion looks like an effective and efficient response for many young offenders. Its effectiveness can only be properly judged with comparable groups, however, and it delivers justice only if every young person has fair access to it.

questions.text: With reference to the hypothetical scenario, explain how the International Criminal Court could deal with the alleged crimes, and the limits it would face.

stimulus.title: Hypothetical scenario: the conflict in Veldoria
stimulus.body:
This scenario is invented for practice. Veldoria and Marenta are fictional states.

During a civil war in Veldoria, a rebel commander, Colonel Arak, is accused of ordering attacks on villages in which civilians were deliberately killed, and of recruiting children aged 12 and 13 into his forces. Veldoria has ratified the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (1998). Its courts have stopped functioning in the areas affected by the war, and no national investigation has begun.

Colonel Arak has fled to neighbouring Marenta, which is not a party to the Rome Statute and has said it will not hand him over to any international court.
evidence_titles: Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (1998)

criteria.descriptor: Explains accurately how the ICC's jurisdiction, ways of starting a case and admissibility rules apply to the scenario, and the practical and legal limits it faces, with reference to relevant law
Explains some ways the ICC could act, with some reference to the scenario and its limits
Provides general information about the ICC

required_elements: Crimes within jurisdiction: war crimes (attacks on civilians; using children under 15), possibly crimes against humanity
Jurisdiction based on the crimes occurring on a state party's territory; how a case can start
Admissibility: complementarity is satisfied because Veldoria is unable to act and has not acted
Limits: reliance on state cooperation for arrest; Marenta is not a party; the accused must be present at trial
A relevant example, such as the Lubanga case
questions.model:
The International Criminal Court could well have jurisdiction over Colonel Arak. Actually getting him into a courtroom is another matter, because that depends on cooperation he is unlikely to face.

The alleged conduct falls within the Court's subject-matter jurisdiction under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (1998). Deliberately attacking civilians is a war crime, and if the attacks were part of a widespread or systematic attack on a civilian population they could also be crimes against humanity. Recruiting children under 15 into armed forces or groups is also a war crime. In Prosecutor v Thomas Lubanga Dyilo (ICC, 2012) the Court convicted a militia leader of enlisting and conscripting children under 15, so this charge has a clear precedent.

The Court would have jurisdiction because the crimes were committed on the territory of Veldoria, a state party; it does not matter that Arak has since left. A case could begin through a referral by Veldoria, by the Prosecutor acting on their own initiative with the approval of the Court's judges, or by a Security Council referral.

The case would be admissible as well. Under the principle of complementarity, the Court acts only where states are unwilling or unable genuinely to investigate or prosecute. Veldoria's courts are not functioning in the affected areas and no national investigation has begun, so the Court would not be displacing a genuine national process.

Enforcement is where it falls down. The Court has no police force and relies on states to arrest and surrender suspects. Marenta is not a party to the Rome Statute and has refused to cooperate, so it has no treaty obligation to hand Arak over unless the Security Council imposes one. Because an accused must be present for trial, an arrest warrant could remain unenforced for years. The Court's response would therefore depend on diplomatic pressure, on Arak travelling to a state willing to arrest him, or on other states prosecuting him under their own laws.
evidence_titles: Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (1998)

questions.text: With reference to the hypothetical draft charter in the stimulus, explain how it reflects different types of human rights.

stimulus.title: Hypothetical scenario: a draft charter of rights for the fictional Republic of Talmar
stimulus.body:
This draft is invented for practice. Talmar is a fictional state.

Article 1. Every person has the right to vote in free elections and to stand for public office.

Article 2. Every person has the right to free primary and secondary education.

Article 3. The Indigenous peoples of Talmar have the right to determine their own political status and to pursue their economic, social and cultural development.

Article 4. Every person has the right to a healthy environment.

Article 5. The rights in Articles 2 and 4 are to be achieved progressively, as the resources of the Republic allow.

criteria.descriptor: Explains accurately how the draft charter reflects civil and political rights, economic, social and cultural rights, and collective rights, linking each to international instruments and explaining progressive realisation
Explains several types of rights in the draft, with relevant links
Describes some types of rights in the draft
Identifies one or two types of rights
Provides some relevant information

required_elements: Article 1 as a civil and political right
Article 2 as an economic, social and cultural right, and progressive realisation in Article 5
Article 3 as the collective right of self-determination
Article 4 as an emerging environmental right
Why the types differ (individual or collective; immediate or progressive)
questions.model:
The draft charter covers the main types of human rights recognised in international law, and the way it treats each type closely follows the international instruments.

Article 1 protects civil and political rights: the right to vote and to stand for office. They are individual rights that protect a person's participation in government and are set out in the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966). They are generally expected to be respected immediately.

Article 2 protects an economic, social and cultural right, the right to education, which appears in the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (1966). Article 5 makes this right subject to progressive realisation 'as the resources of the Republic allow', which mirrors that Covenant's approach: states must take steps, to the maximum of their available resources, towards fully realising these rights, recognising that they often require significant public spending.

Article 3 is different because it is a collective right. Self-determination belongs to peoples rather than individuals and appears in Article 1 of both covenants. Its application to Indigenous peoples is recognised in the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (2007), which is influential but not a binding treaty.

Article 4 goes further again, reflecting an emerging right to a healthy environment. It is collective in nature, because environmental harm affects whole communities and future generations, and it is not set out in the core UN human rights treaties, which shows how the recognition of rights continues to develop. Including it in Article 5 also treats it as a right to be achieved over time.

What the draft shows, then, is that rights differ both in who holds them and in how quickly states are expected to deliver them.

International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (1966)
United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (2007)

required_elements: Pregnancy discrimination in employment is unlawful under federal and NSW law
A complaint to the Australian Human Rights Commission: free, informal, confidential conciliation
If conciliation fails: court proceedings, with cost and publicity concerns
The alternative NSW avenue under the Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 (NSW)
A judgement about effectiveness for Ana (accessibility against the limits of an individual complaints model)
questions.model:
For someone in Ana's position the domestic mechanisms work reasonably well, because they are accessible and confidential. Their weakness is that they rely on her complaining and on the company agreeing to settle.

The company seems to have broken the law. The Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth) makes discrimination on the ground of pregnancy unlawful in employment, including in deciding who is offered a job. The Act implements Australia's obligations under the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (1979), so Ana's situation shows an international standard being enforced through domestic law.

Ana's first step would be a complaint to the Australian Human Rights Commission, which operates under the Australian Human Rights Commission Act 1986 (Cth). That suits her well. It is free and does not require a lawyer, which matters because she cannot afford one. The Commission investigates and tries to resolve complaints through conciliation, a confidential process that avoids the publicity she fears, and outcomes can include an apology, compensation or a change to the employer's practices.

The limits show up if the company digs in. Conciliation depends on the company's willingness to settle, and the Commission cannot make a binding decision. If conciliation fails, Ana would have to take the matter to court, where proceedings are public, slower and more expensive, and where she might risk paying costs. The system also places the burden on the individual: it responds to Ana's complaint but does little on its own to change the attitudes behind the decision.

Ana could instead use the state system under the Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 (NSW), which also covers pregnancy discrimination and offers a free complaints process, with the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal available if the complaint is not resolved.

These mechanisms are effective in giving Ana an accessible, low-cost and private avenue. If the company refuses to cooperate, though, they become much less effective, because her final remedy then depends on costly and public litigation.

questions.text: With reference to the hypothetical scenario, evaluate the effectiveness of legal and non-legal responses to the use of child soldiers.

stimulus.title: Hypothetical scenario: child soldiers in the fictional state of Korvan
stimulus.body:
This scenario is invented for practice. Korvan is a fictional state.

An armed opposition group in Korvan's northern provinces has recruited several hundred children, some as young as 11, to serve as fighters, messengers and guards. Korvan is a party to the Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989), the Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child on the involvement of children in armed conflict (2000) and the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (1998).

An international NGO has published interviews with former child soldiers, and the story has been covered widely by international media. A UN agency is running a program to help released children return to school and their families. Korvan's government says it cannot reach the northern provinces to arrest the group's leaders.

Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child on the involvement of children in armed conflict (2000)
Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (1998)

criteria.descriptor: Makes an informed judgement about the effectiveness of legal and non-legal responses to child soldiers; applies relevant international law accurately to the scenario; weighs strengths and limitations of each response
Makes a sound judgement with relevant legal and non-legal examples
Describes legal and/or non-legal responses with some reference to the scenario
Provides general information about child soldiers or human rights

required_elements: Treaty standards: the CRC (age 15) and the Optional Protocol (under 18 for armed groups)
International criminal law: the war crime of using children under 15; complementarity; the Lubanga case
Enforcement limits: the state cannot reach the area; the ICC relies on arrests by states
Non-legal responses: NGO documentation, media pressure, reintegration programs
An explicit overall judgement
questions.model:
In Korvan the law is clear about what is forbidden and who can be held responsible, but it is only partly effective, because enforcing it needs a control over the north that Korvan simply does not have. Non-legal responses fill important gaps, especially in helping children recover, but they cannot stop recruitment by themselves.

On paper the treaty framework is strong. As a party to the Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989), Korvan must take all feasible measures to ensure that children under 15 do not take a direct part in hostilities, and must not recruit them into its armed forces. The Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child on the involvement of children in armed conflict (2000) goes further, providing that armed groups distinct from a state's armed forces should not recruit or use people under 18 in hostilities, and requiring states to take measures to prevent this. The opposition group is clearly in breach of these standards. However, these treaties bind states, and Korvan cannot enforce them in provinces it does not control.

International criminal law aims at the individuals responsible. Under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (1998), enlisting or conscripting children under 15, or using them to participate actively in hostilities, is a war crime. Because the crimes occurred in Korvan, a state party, and Korvan is unable to arrest or prosecute the leaders, the case would be admissible under the principle of complementarity. Prosecutor v Thomas Lubanga Dyilo (ICC, 2012) shows that such prosecutions can succeed. Yet the Court relies on states to arrest suspects, so while the leaders remain beyond Korvan's reach, an arrest warrant may achieve little except to restrict their travel. In addition, the war crime covers only children under 15, so the recruitment of 15 to 17-year-olds depends on the weaker treaty standard.

The non-legal responses work in other ways. The NGO's interviews document abuses, raise awareness and may later provide evidence for prosecutors. Media coverage can build international pressure on the group and on states that support it. The UN agency's program addresses a need the law cannot meet: helping children recover, return to school and reunite with their families. These responses, however, depend on funding and access, and they cannot compel the group to stop.

Legal and non-legal responses are therefore only partly effective. The law establishes that recruiting children is unlawful and that leaders can be prosecuted, while non-legal measures support victims and keep the issue visible. Their combined effectiveness will ultimately depend on Korvan regaining control of the north or on the leaders being arrested.
